summary: Describes Multi Access Management Services (MAMS), a framework for devices that can use several networks at once, such as Wi-Fi, LTE and DSL. It lets a client and network smartly select and combine access paths and adapt as conditions change, to improve user experience and network efficiency.

eli5.summary: Your phone can reach the internet through Wi-Fi and a cell signal. This describes a way to use both at once, choosing the best road for each trip.

subtitle: Framework for intelligent path selection when devices have multiple network connections

tldr.problem: Devices can now connect to multiple networks (Wi-Fi, LTE, DSL) simultaneously, but lack a unified way to intelligently choose which network to use for different types of traffic, adapt to changing conditions, and aggregate capacity across multiple paths.
tldr.mechanism: MAMS defines a control-plane protocol and user-plane architecture with separate functional components at the client and network that negotiate path selection, user-plane protocols, and traffic steering rules based on application needs and network conditions.
tldr.outcome: Devices and networks can dynamically optimize which network paths to use for each direction of traffic, with support for aggregating capacity, switching without packet loss, and transparent operation across different access technologies.

facts.label: Control protocol
facts.value: WebSocket over TCP/TLS with JSON messages

today: RFC 8743 is an Informational document published in March 2020 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It serves as the foundation for related work on MAMS protocol extensions and protocol-specific applications. While the RFC does not represent IETF consensus, it is widely referenced for multiconnectivity management principles.

sections.title: Multiconnectivity and Path Selection
sections.content:
Multi-Access Management Services (MAMS) is a framework that lets devices with multiple network connections intelligently choose which networks to use for their traffic. Modern devices can connect via Wi-Fi, LTE, 5G, DSL, and other technologies simultaneously. Each technology has different characteristics: Wi-Fi offers high throughput when coverage is good but degrades near edges; cellular networks provide predictable quality under licensed spectrum; DSL offers fixed high capacity. MAMS provides mechanisms to select the best combination of access paths and core networks, configure how data flows across them, and adapt dynamically as conditions change.

The framework operates transparently across different access technologies and does not depend on any specific network type or user-plane protocol. This makes it future-proof, allowing new access technologies and transport protocols to be integrated without redesign.
sections.eli5: Your devices have access to many networks. MAMS gives them smart rules to pick the best network for each kind of traffic, and to use multiple networks together when needed.

sections.title: Why Multipath Management Matters
sections.content: Different access networks have complementary strengths and weaknesses. In good Wi-Fi coverage, users get high throughput. As they move toward the edge of coverage or encounter congestion, performance degrades rapidly. LTE networks provide lower peak throughput but more predictable service. Additionally, the choice of access network often determines which services are reachable: enterprise printers and video conferencing may only work via a corporate Wi-Fi core, while public internet services flow through the operator's LTE core. Without a unified framework, applications must adapt to whatever network is available, leading to poor user experience. MAMS lets the network and client work together to choose paths that optimize performance for each application's needs, whether that means maximum throughput, low latency, or reliable connectivity.
sections.eli5: WiFi is fast but spotty. Cell service is slow but steady. MAMS helps pick the right one for each app, or use both together.

sections.title: Reference Architecture and Functional Components
sections.content:
MAMS separates control-plane and user-plane functions. At the client, the Client Connection Manager (CCM) handles control signaling, and the Client Multi-Access Data Proxy (C-MADP) forwards user traffic across multiple network paths. In the network, the Network Connection Manager (NCM) negotiates with the client and configures the network-side functions, while the Network Multi-Access Data Proxy (N-MADP) distributes traffic across multiple access networks and core networks.

The NCM and CCM exchange control messages as user-plane data using WebSocket over TCP/TLS, so control signaling requires no special network support and is independent of the underlying access technologies. The N-MADP forwards uplink traffic to the appropriate core network (anchor connection) and downlink traffic to the client over the appropriate access links (delivery connections). This architecture supports multiple deployment scenarios: co-located or distributed components, multiple N-MADP instances for load balancing or different applications, and flexible use of different user-plane protocols for different paths.
sections.eli5: On the phone, one part talks to the network and one part picks which connection to use. On the network side, one part sets policy and one part forwards traffic. They talk in secret so no one else sees.

sections.title: Control Plane and User Plane Protocols
sections.content:
The MAMS user-plane consists of two layers: a Convergence Layer that handles multi-access-specific functions like path selection, aggregation, fragmentation, concatenation, reordering and lossless switching; and an optional Adaptation Layer that handles reachability and security such as tunneling, IPsec encryption, and NAT traversal. The Convergence Layer can be implemented using existing protocols like MPTCP (RFC 6824), QUIC, GRE (RFC 2784), or custom schemes. The Adaptation Layer can use IPsec, DTLS, or client-side NAT, and can be configured independently for each access link (for example, encryption for Wi-Fi but not for trusted LTE).

The control plane uses JSON-formatted messages over WebSocket for discovery, capability exchange, user-plane configuration, path quality estimation, traffic steering, and measurement reporting. Key procedures include: the client discovering the NCM and exchanging supported features; configuration of user-plane protocols and protocols for each access path; periodic probing of path quality; and steering of traffic flows based on application requirements and network policy.
sections.eli5: Two layers handle data: one picks the best network, the other encrypts or tunnels data if needed. Control messages are JSON packages asking "what do you support?" and saying "use this path now."

sections.title: Negotiation and Dynamic Adaptation
sections.content:
MAMS operation begins with discovery: the CCM sends an MX Discover message to the NCM, which responds with system information including the available anchor connections (core networks) and their types. The CCM then sends a capability exchange request listing supported features such as lossless switching, fragmentation, aggregation, and measurement. The NCM responds with its capabilities and sets up the user-plane configuration with the credentials and protocols for the C-MADP and N-MADP to use.

After setup, the client and network exchange path quality information: the client probes access links by sending probe packets and reporting back results, or the NCM actively probes paths. Based on this information and network policies, the NCM sends traffic steering directives to the client, specifying which flows or packets should use which access paths. The framework supports policy-based selection, allowing both client-local policies and network-delivered policies. A keep-alive procedure detects failures and recovers from dead-peer scenarios. When network conditions change, the client reports new measurements and the NCM adapts the path selection and user-plane treatment.
sections.eli5: First, the phone and network say hello and swap abilities. Next, they pick which networks to use and how to protect data. Then they test the connections and adjust if needed.

sections.title: Deployment Flexibility and Security
sections.content:
MAMS requires no changes to underlying access networks or their signaling procedures. LTE and Wi-Fi continue using their native protocols; MAMS control messages are carried as user-plane data transparently. The NCM collects topology information (via BGP-LS or similar) and traffic information from network management systems; it can compute optimal paths within seconds and react to network changes within minutes. Different deployment models are possible: the NCM and N-MADP can be collocated or separate, multiple N-MADP instances can handle different client sets or application types, and a single client can use multiple N-MADP instances for TCP and UDP traffic separately.

Security relies on TLS protection of the control channel and optional encryption of user data via the Adaptation Layer. The centralized control point (NCM) is a potential attack target and must be protected. If communication between client and NCM is disrupted, the client reverts to native single-path operation, recovering automatically when the connection is restored.
sections.eli5: Networks don't need to change. The controller watches for problems and reacts in seconds. If the controller dies, phones go back to using one network. Different parts can be on different servers.
